newsitem.title: NEW ZEALAND: NZ BILL YIELDS CLOSE HIGHER, KIWI ENDS LOWER.
newsitem.headline: NZ BILL YIELDS CLOSE HIGHER, KIWI ENDS LOWER.

text.p: Figures in brackets compare against previous day's close
FUTURES PHYSICAL YIELD (PCT)
90-DAY BILLS (SEP) 92.01 (PREV 92.10) 90-DAYS 8.35 (PREV 8.21)
OVERNIGHT CASH 8.10 PCT (PREV 8.15) US 5-YR 6.10 (PREV 6.12)
RBNZ MCI NZ/MCI 741.96 (PREV 744.25) Reuters NZ MCI -83 vs -78
New Zealand bank bill yields sharply closed higher on Thursday in response to a weaker New Zealand dollar Trade Weighted Index.
Bonds also weakened in a slow session dominated by a poorly bid $150 million government bond tender.
There was heavy trade in the kiwi with four local banks slugging it out on behalf of Asian sellers and U.S. buyers.
The kiwi ended at US$0.6405/12, little changed from its opening but above the 17 month low of 0.6388 touched overnight.
A Wellington bank dealer said the kiwi showed no liking for the 0.6422 session topside and quickly went to test 0.6405.
He said it appeared the sellers gained the ascendancy and he expects further downside overnight.

There was mild interest in the currency market in the sacking of Associate Health Minister Neil Kirton. Dealers said it was a negative for the dollar, showing further instability within the governing coalition.

However, bond dealers put a different complexion on it, saying it showed the prime minister Jim Bolger and Deputy Prime Minister Winston Peters acting decisively. Also, they said even if Kirton joined the opposition, it would not affect the government's ability to rule.
The weak currency was the main reason for the bills to be sold and the kiwi's direction would determine direction in the short end.
The Monetary Conditions Index remained around 85 points easier than the Reserve Bank's desired level and the weakening TWI had the bill market struggling not to let the easing go too far.

Weak bidding of only $228 million for the government's $150 million government bond tender reflected concerns about the global environment for bonds and the fact that foreign investors are already long in bonds.
"There's not a lot of room for them to buy a lot more," said the chief bond dealer of a Wellington bank.
"We are approaching the top end of recent rates but the market is range trading and not showing any great momentum either way."
